content: Luminous intensity, in the field of photometry, is a measure of the wavelength-weighted power emitted by a light source in a specific direction. This measurement is based on the luminosity function, which is a standardized model representing the sensitivity of the human eye to different wavelengths of light. The SI unit for luminous intensity is the candela (cd), which is one of the base units in the International System of Units (SI). Photometry focuses on the measurement of visible light as perceived by the human eye. The human eye is only capable of detecting light within the visible spectrum and exhibits varying sensitivities to different wavelengths within this range. Under bright lighting conditions, known as photopic vision, the human eye is most sensitive to greenish-yellow light with a wavelength of 555 nm. Light of the same radiant intensity at other wavelengths appears to have a lower luminous intensity to the human eye. The response of the human eye to light is quantified by a standardized curve called the luminosity function, denoted as V(λ) or ȳ(λ). This curve is derived from an average of experimental data collected by scientists using various measurement techniques. For example, the measured response of the eye to violet light has been found to vary by a factor of ten across different experiments. It is important to distinguish luminous intensity from other photometric units, such as luminous flux. Luminous flux represents the total perceived power emitted by a light source in all directions, whereas luminous intensity refers to the perceived power per unit solid angle in a specific direction. Additionally, luminous intensity is distinct from radiant intensity, which is the corresponding objective physical quantity used in radiometry, a field concerned with the measurement of electromagnetic radiation. The candela, like other SI base units, has an operational definition. It is defined by describing a physical process that produces one candela of luminous intensity. Specifically, if a light source emits monochromatic light at a frequency of 540 THz (corresponding to a wavelength of approximately 555 nm, near the peak sensitivity of the human eye) and has a radiant intensity of 1/683 watts per steradian in a given direction, that light source is said to emit one candela in the specified direction. If such a source emitted light uniformly in all directions, it would produce a total power output of approximately 40 milliwatts. For reference, a typical candle emits roughly one candela of luminous intensity. Historically, in 1881, Jules Violle proposed the Violle as a unit of luminous intensity. This was significant as it was the first unit of light intensity that did not rely on the properties of a specific lamp. However, the Violle was eventually replaced by the candela in 1946.
